proposals.relationship: Labrousse identifies an economic rereading of Marx, equipped by Simiand and Aftalion’s methods and checked against historical evidence, as a formative resource.
proposals.evidence_note: Own interview 112–113 explicitly describes his methodological relationship to Simiand, says he never followed Simiand’s teaching, and credits Simiand and Aftalion with instruments for rereading Marx from 1925. Their roles and the historical control are integral, not Marx as sole source or a direct teacher. He acknowledges only indirect Durkheim exposure. Own 123 rejects automatic economic causation and an absolute impoverishment thesis he calls unfaithful to Marxism; this is not blanket doctrinal agreement. Interviews recorded late 1978/early 1979 and published 1980; original Marx works and private seminar records remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Labrousse takes up Febvre’s economies, societies and civilizations formula to explain a program of interrelated collective forces and changing research priorities.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Annales answer 114 explicitly attributes the three-term formula to Febvre, stresses their interrelations and shifting emphases rather than an unchanging hierarchy, and on 115 calls the triple watchword his operational strategy. This is a particular programmatic use, not formal supervision, invention of all social history or endorsement of every Febvre argument. His acknowledgment of individual agency and complementarity with cultural history remains. No complete Febvre text newly read.
primary_locators: 1980 interview printed114, Les Annales answer, and115 final methodological paragraph; actual114 visually collated

proposals.relationship: Labrousse invokes Braudel’s Mediterranean study as an exemplary account of collective forces shaping apparently freer political and individual history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 114 Annales answer singles out Braudel’s Philippe II as an enduring example while insisting that collective history need not suppress the individual. Charle’s note4 identifies La Méditerranée and its 1966 second edition, separately recording 1949 first publication. The exemplar supports a bounded conceptual resource, not proof of first-reading date, formal mentoring or equal rhythms for all historical forces. Original Braudel monograph remains unread. This incoming resource is distinct from the existing reverse Labrousse-to-Braudel contribution 445.
primary_locators: 1980 interview printed114, paragraph beginning Le grand lien commun, note4; actual page visually collated

proposals.relationship: Braudel questions Labrousse’s return toward short-duration revolutionary crises while praising his work and accepting the usefulness of connecting economic and political events.
proposals.evidence_note: Actual original 1958 pages 730–731 contrast Labrousse’s 1933 secular price inquiry with the shorter revolutionary-crisis inquiry and especially Comment naissent les révolutions? 1948. Braudel calls the operation legitimate and useful but symptomatic of a return to short time, alongside exceptionally strong praise of La Crise. He also says social and economic conjunctures need not move at identical speeds. This is a particular temporal disagreement, not rejection of Labrousse’s research or an independently proved failure. Braudel’s 1943 dating is preserved as his printed wording; the graph’s separately established 1944 book publication is unchanged. Original Labrousse monographs and 1948 paper remain unread.
